HI, I have a problem in a project where none of the usual collection types seem an exactly correct solution. I'm wondering if anyone knows if what I'm describing already has a name.

A collection S where

  • order is irrelevant
  • heterogenous elements, where all types are known
  • only 1 element per type (unique types, not just unique values). While a normal Set would allow {1,2,"foo"} because 1 and 2 are distinct values. my S would only allow {1,"foo"} as only a single occurrence of Nat is allowed. In other words. the length of S corresponds exactly to the number of types in S. A homogenous S will always have length = 1.

It's set-like in that it is unordered and has no duplicates, but it's also tuple-like in that it has an exactly known size (by looking at the number of types it contains).

structure Foo where
  n : Nat
structure Bar where
  s : String
def ex1 : S [Foo Bar] = [Foo.mk 3, Bar.mk "str"] -- ✅
def ex2 : S [Foo Bar] = [Bar.mk "str", Foo.mk 3] -- ✅
#eval ex1 == ex2 -- ✅ true
val bad : S[Foo, Bar] = [Bar.mk "str", Foo(3), Foo(1)] -- ❌ multiple occurrences of Foo. Either errors or silently discards

What should I call this? And more importantly, is this possible to implement in Lean4
What do you mean "unique types"? If I def MyNat := Nat, then is the collection allowed to contain both an element of Nat and an element of MyNat?

Aaron Liu said:

What do you mean "unique types"? If I def MyNat := Nat, then is the collection allowed to contain both an element of Nat and an element of MyNat?

I assume that would be the same as saying abbrev MyNat := Nat, just "another way of saying Nat", not nominally distinct, so I would say that it's not allowed. Although if Lean actually treats def type aliases as nominally distinct then I'm also fine with it being allowed - this ambiguity will not come up practically in my real problem so I'm okay with either policy.
Sounds like DHashMap Type* id, but with a map that doesn't require hashable

import Mathlib
open Classical
instance : Hashable Type* := sorry
-- TODO: replace `DHashMap` with a key-value store that doesn't require `Hashable`
abbrev Collection := Std.DHashMap Type* id
it's not possible to index a collection by Type* because given a value of Type* you know nothing about there's no way to extract any information computably

With a Map, will the specific types remain known, beyond Type*? Such that I could a define functions that only accept an S Int String? 

def ex1 : S [Int Str] = [1, "hello"]
def f (x : S Int Str) := ()

f ex1
Well you could always accept proofs that the collection satisfies whatever you want, but no it wouldn't be in the type itself (i.e. it's bundled)
with docs#Dynamic, Lean is able to be indexing stuff by Type* anyways, but that's because it's using docs#TypeName as a stand-in for the type

I've (with AI help) implemented an HList that is able to retain all of the types of elements as information

inductive HList : List Type → Type 1 where
  | nil  : HList []
  | cons : {α : Type} → {αs : List Type} → α → HList αs → HList (α :: αs)

But this is a List, while what I want seems more like a Set
it's not clear to me how you plan to index into this set
since it's unordered, you can't use the position in the ordering to pick out an element

By the type

def s : S [Int Str] = [1, "hello"]
#eval s.get Int -- 1
types are erased at compilation time, so from the compiler's perspective you're passing in no data
there's also the problem that values aren't tagged with their type, so you could have values of different types having the same internal representation
I have this working locally
will paste code

Could you please speak a bit more about the practicalities/real problem you mentioned earlier?

There are various technical obstructions to having a thing like this on the nose (for example, how can you enforce types appearing uniquely when there are models of lean where every type of the same cardinality is equal, iirc? :grinning_face_with_smiling_eyes:), but I think there’s probably a way to #xy if you are trying to address practical concerns.

I am new to Lean, and new to using inductive types and typeclasses, but this is what I was able to get working with AI help 

inductive HList : List Type → Type 1 where
  | nil  : HList []
  | cons : {α : Type} → {αs : List Type} → α → HList αs → HList (α :: αs)

instance {α : Type} {αs : List Type} : HAdd (HList αs) α (HList (α :: αs)) where
  hAdd xs a := HList.cons a xs

class HGet (α : Type) (αs : List Type) : Type 1 where
  get : HList αs → α

instance (α : Type) (αs : List Type) : HGet α (α :: αs) where
  get
    | HList.cons a _ => a

instance (α : Type) (β : Type) (αs : List Type) [HGet α αs] : HGet α (β :: αs) where
  get
    | HList.cons _ xs => HGet.get (α := α) xs

def HList.get {αs : List Type} (xs : HList αs) (α : Type) [HGet α αs] : α :=
  HGet.get (α := α) xs

infixr:67 " h:: " => HList.cons
def s : HList [Int, String] := 1 h:: "hi" h:: HList.nil

#eval s.get Int
#eval s.get String
I hope it's not incoherent AI hallucination. It seems to work.
oh, I thought you figured out a way to make it unordered too

Ah no not yet, that is my current desire.

But this is a List, while what I want seems more like a Set
the version you posted should be working when your types aren't too complicated and your list isn't too long and as long as you don't add in any duplicated yourself

I managed to get it feeling unordered in usage, the AI did this by generating some things called "projections"

class HProject (βs : List Type) (αs : List Type) : Type 1 where
  project : HList αs → HList βs

instance (αs : List Type) : HProject [] αs where
  project _ := HList.nil

instance (β : Type) (βs : List Type) (αs : List Type) [HGet β αs] [HProject βs αs] : HProject (β :: βs) αs where
  project xs :=
    HList.cons (HGet.get (α := β) xs) (HProject.project (βs := βs) xs)

instance (αs : List Type) (βs : List Type) [HProject βs αs] : CoeTC (HList αs) (HList βs) where
  coe xs := HProject.project (βs := βs) xs

def f(s : HList [Int, String]) := s
def g(s : HList [String, Int]) := s

#check f (g s)

Is this a legitimate approach?

Interesting! One issue with this overall approach—not sure if it’s relevant to your problem—is that the instance of HGet is decided at compile time. So you can’t get the Int element of an arbitrary HList types where types : List Type is a free variable that you merely know contains Int somewhere, for example. You would need to be dealing with a specific explicit list of types for it to behave as you expect.
also it doesn't prevent you from adding duplicates to your List Type and it starts behaving badly as soon as you do have duplicates
I would definitely encourage you to #xy a bit, as whether it’s a legitimate approach depends very much on what you’re trying to approach and why :grinning_face_with_smiling_eyes:

maybe I'm confused, but wouldn't this work?

import Mathlib.Tactic

universe u

abbrev TypeValue : Type (u + 1) := (α : Type u) × α

structure TypeValueSet where
  S : Set TypeValue
  no_dup : ∀ (x y : TypeValue), x ∈ S → y ∈ S → x.1 = y.1 → x = y

Could you please speak a bit more about the practicalities/real problem you mentioned earlier?

Sure. I'm trying to model an Entity in a video game or simulation, where Entities often can sort of belong to many different types at once (things that are physical, things that have health and stamina, things that can be drawn to the screen, etc). Rather than using multiple-inheritance, I want to say, as a type of ECS pattern, that an Entity is simply a Set of structures that define it's aspects. (In this case. HList is the "Set", so Entity is just an HList)

structure Physics where
  position : Vector Float 3
  velocity : Vector Float 3
  mass     : Float

structure Stats where
  health : Float
  stamina : Float

structure Graphics where
  spritepath : String


def player := Physics mk [0,0,0] [0,0,0] 0 h:: Stats.mk 100 100 h:: Graphics.mk "player.png"

here the type of Player is HList [Physics, Stats, Graphics], and I can pass it to functions that transform Physics by saying f (player.get Physics).

This is very similar to multi-inheritance, but will allow me to arbitrarily build anonymous entities and remove and add types to the same entity during the runtime in a generalized way, which is important in some video games.

instance {α : Type} {αs : List Type} : HAdd (HList αs) α (HList (α :: αs)) where
  hAdd xs a := HList.cons a xs

So I can take an entity e of type HList [Physics, Stats, Graphics] and run e add Inventory.m 10 to produce a new entity of type HList [Physics, Stats, Graphics, Inventory]who can now have an inventory of items

The goal after this would be to build infrastructure for taking a list of functions that operate of structures (like Physics, or Stats), and loop through a list of entities (a bunch of HLists) and automatically update every relevant aspect of every entity.
why would a Player lack Physics or Stats

A player would not, but you may have other entities that share some aspects as the Player but lack others. A Rock is Physical but has no Stats. The physics functions should treat the player and the rock the same.
so do you know all the possible types you could put into an Entity at compile time
maybe I'm skimming over this too quickly, but it sounds like you just want a hash map

so do you know all the possible types you could put into an Entity at compile time

Would have to clarify exactly what this means. As a game engine, users should be able to define their own aspects (not just Physical and Stats) and their own functions that update them, and add them to whatever entities they want whenever they want.

Oh, that’s really interesting! Hmmm… “adding aspects during the runtime” suggests to me that you need a different approach than the current one, at least, but there is probably an approach that does what you want here. Adding things at runtime also makes me think that perhaps you do not want these aspects to be parameters in the type, as that restricts what functions you can write.

when you say "users" do you mean "people who are using the game engine to write games" or "people who are playing some game"

it sounds like this is just a compile time thing, unless you're talking about software that runs and prompts the user (in a terminal or in a GUI) to come up with aspects and functions

Game developers, users of the engine. Though I also think users, if the game exposes some sort of console system like Skyrim has, should be able to trigger it through console commands. like by typing finding out the id of an entity in the world - lets say 1 - and writing add_aspect physics (...) entity_id=1 in the console
but would "physics" be a pre-existing thing or something that the player created and named during the game as it was running

Physics would be pre-coded by the developer. Yeah I'm not sure how the lookup would be, maybe the developer would have to manually maintain a list of all components that exist to ship with each build, as String literals, maybe some macro or reflection if possible in Lean. But anyway, that's just a bonus goal, the main objective is just letting developers add whatever types they want to entities in compile checked functions they give to the engine before building

Just as an example video game I like to give whenever people are confused by how general and dynamic I'm wanting this (indeed the vast majority of games do not need to have something as extreme as this).

Imagine it's a spellcasting magic game. You have a Banana (a physical, edible item), and you cast a spell that gives consciousness to the Banana, so now you have a banana that can walk and talk (physical, edible, NPC) etc. Things like that.
I think I agree with @Snir Broshi that you're just looking for docs#Std.DHashMap
(initially wrote the docs link wrong, since fixed it)

Thomas Murrills said:

Adding things at runtime also makes me think that perhaps you do not want these aspects to be parameters in the type, as that restricts what functions you can write.

I want to write functions like

def move : Physics → Physics :=
  λ p => {p with position := p.position + p.velocity}

def friction : Physics → Physics :=
  λ p => {p with velocity := p.velocity * 0.96}

def hunger : Stats → Stats :=
  λ s := {s with health := s.health - 0.00001]

and then define entities like

def player := Physics mk [0,0,0] [0,0,0] 0 h:: Stats.mk 100 100 h:: Grapics.mk "player.png"
def rock := Physics mk [0,0,0] [0,0,0] 0 h:: Grapics.mk "rock.png"
def nonphysical_ghost := NPC.mk Personality.hostile h:: ...

and have both aggregated in collections entities and transformations

def entities = [player, rock, nonphysical_ghost]
def transformations = [move, friction, hunger]

and then every frame, iterate through both lists, one function with one entity at a time, (f, e) and ask "does this entity have the type that this function operates on?", and if so, update that new entity using the function, e' := f e. If not, skip.
This seems to be the hardest part as it requires be being totally unspecific about what types of entities might exist, corresponding the right entities to the right transformation function has to be a runtime check - otherwise the developer has to write lots and lots of tedious routing logic. But this is clearly a formalizable problem, so I would expect it to be possible in Lean. Something like "given an f : α → α and an x : (HList β), if β = α, then apply f (x.get β)"

And of course, I must be able to add and remove entities and transformations during the runtime. Like if I were to want to suddenly disable physics for a few moments. I would remove move from transformations so all entities positions stop being updated.

does this entity have the type that this function operates on?

using a DHashMap, that would just be type ∈ entity

But this loses type information, so if I did want to explicitly call move (player.get Physics), it isn't typesafe. Or it uses Option, which isn't good because we know for certain that Physics is there.
If I define a player as having Physics, it should be known to the type system that player.get Physics is safe.
And if I put the player in a list of other entities (which may or may not have Physics), I should be able to loop through that list and apply move to every entity that has Physics
That collections can't have unknowns or type unions is making this very difficult. I've gotten it working this far in Scala before.
if h : Physics ∈ player then move (player.get Physics h) else [do something else]?
what's wrong with the above conditional

Because we know that Physics is in player because we wrote that in it's instantiation

def player := Physics mk [0,0,0] [0,0,0] 0 h:: ...

#eval move (player.get Physics)
So the conditional would force users to write tedious checks for things that are already known
you can use decide then, I think (could be wrong though)
I'm struggling to even see how I would construct a player with Physics using the Hashmap approaches. The LLMs are giving me code that requires lots of repetitive hardcoding for things like typename.

I notice that you keep formatting this data structure as a list, but isn't it just a key-value map with optional keys? viewing it as a list of key-value pairs with an arbitrary order and restrictions on key uniqueness seems like a map with extra steps
I would imagine that the Player definition would look more like { Physics := ..., Stats := ... }
(actually I'm not sure if you can use that notation with DHashMap, so perhaps not...)
anyway, perhaps it's the wrong approach

Well I was viewing it as a List of structure instances, where the List remembers which types the structures were, and hoping that I could just ask in the runtime what those types were. But I am fine with whichever underlying representation is used, so long as

  • its known at the type level which aspects an entity has
  • It can be asked in the runtime what aspects an element has, and if a given function has the domain of that type

I want to underscore that, beyond sets or lists or maps, the real goal here is implementing something that feels like multiple inheritance, but with the ability to add or remove types during the runtime (by producting a new entity that has more or fewer types)

Matt Diamond said:

I would imagine that the Player definition would look more like { Physics := ..., Stats := ... }

And if I wanted to add components to Player, or remove one, like removing Physics?
are you referring to adding components to a specific player or to the player type?

Well I am hesitant to talk about a "player type" since in ECS there are really no rigid "types" of entities, an entity is just a composition of a number of aspects or "components". What distinguishes a player from a rock is only that it has more aspects, like intelligence (though a magic spell might make a rock become intelligent for a few minutes in the game). The only thing that a player "type" would be, would be an abbrev alias to that composition.

abbrev Player := HList [Physics, Stats, Graphics, Intelligence, Inventory, MouseControllable]
You could even turn a rock into the Player, if you added the MouseControllable structure to it's component list, and maybe a few more like CameraFollow.

ah I see, thanks for explaining... I'm not super familiar with entity component systems so that might be why I'm having trouble conceptualizing this properly

someone else may have better luck here
ECS should probably use hashmaps, plus perfect-hashing for performance

I would have to see what a sketch of that looks like. My interest in ECS isn't the performance or data-oriented mindset like usual, it's only the ability to represent entities as having many different types at once and being able to remove and add more types during the runtime, and I'm okay with taking some performance loss if it means more ergonomics and type knowledge on the user side when defining entities and systems. For example, I strongly prefer thinking about an array-of-structures over a structure-of-arrays, even if its slower.

The more traditional ECS implementations that are motivated by performance and data-oriented thinking typically just represent entities as an ID integer, then do a structure-of-arrays/mapping approach where you have to index an ID into them to get the right component for entities, which makes the ergonomics and type safety worse -- at least I have never seen an implementation that looks good in these areas.

In my approach, because I define an Entity as collection of Components directly, right there (and not indirectly in some other external map I have to index into), I can give the entity to functions immediately, because the components are all right there to extract, and there is no middle-man mapping system I have to go through to query components. I wager this also means I can retain more type information about the entity in more locations.
